label: Blue Note
rationale: Duke Jordan's defining statement as a leader — the bebop pianist from Bird's 1947 quintet, fully matured into a composer of originals ('Flight to Jordan', 'Si-Joya') that became session calls. AllMusic 5 stars (Yanow), Penguin Guide 3 stars. Session gravity is high: Dizzy Reece and Stanley Turrentine at the front of their Blue Note years, Reggie Workman and Art Taylor in the engine room — the personnel network links straight into Jordan (Workman), Page One-era Blue Note, and the Coltrane-adjacent circles Jordan came from.

personnel_record.notes: Single session, August 4, 1960, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs (Blue Note BLP 4046). Producer Alfred Lion per Wikipedia (obs). Engineer not stated in sources consulted; Rudy Van Gelder inferred per contract rule (Blue Note, 1960, Van Gelder Studio). Tracks 7-8 are CD-reissue bonus tracks; 'I Should Care' is Duke Jordan solo piano. Wikipedia does not distinguish whether Reece/Turrentine sit out any original-LP track — quintet scope recorded as all-tracks per its flat personnel list; track_assignments_complete false for that reason. Original LP comprises tracks 1-6, all Jordan originals.

ballot.case_for: This is Duke Jordan's defining statement as a leader — the pianist from Bird's 1947 quintet fully matured into a hard-bop composer, with all six original-LP tracks his own compositions, including 'Flight to Jordan' and 'Si-Joya', which saw some session-call afterlife. Session gravity is exceptional: Stanley Turrentine at the dawn of his Blue Note run, the under-recorded Dizzy Reece, Reggie Workman just before entering Coltrane's orbit, and Art Taylor powering the engine room — recorded August 4, 1960 at Van Gelder with Alfred Lion producing (S1, S3). AllMusic's Scott Yanow awards 5 stars (S2), and the album passes the discovery test cleanly: a warm, swinging, flawlessly executed document of the archetypal 1960 Blue Note sound that bridges 1940s bebop veterans and 1960s hard-bop modernists.
ballot.case_against: Consensus is thin at the level the rubric prizes: the Penguin Guide gives only 3 stars — 'good, but' — and the album is absent from NPR, JazzTimes, and DownBeat canon lists; it is beloved by Blue Note aficionados rather than independently recognized across listing traditions. The lineage signal is essentially absent — it changed nothing that came after, sitting among 1960's crowded landmark field (Soul Station, The Big Beat, Giant Steps) as an excellent date rather than a load-bearing cornerstone. Dossier hygiene is also imperfect: track_assignments_complete is false, relying on Wikipedia's flat personnel list, so we cannot confirm whether Reece and Turrentine lay out on any core track — a small but real gap in the historical record.
ballot.disagreement: The references converged on tier (both contested) but split on urgency: Reference 1 weighted session gravity and Jordan's personal arc heavily enough to lean toward 'strong', treating the album as a genuinely strengthening entry for the era; Reference 2 argued 'consider', holding that the split consensus (AllMusic 5★ vs. Penguin 3★) and the non-load-bearing lineage cap it below that. The ballot reflects the more conservative read given the thin independent-consensus evidence.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John treat this as a legitimate but non-urgent candidate: a superb, era-defining Blue Note session worth including if the collection wants a deep-cut hard-bop quintet date, but not a hole anyone would notice.
